utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, I understand you have a preliminary mater to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Thank you. First of all, it's relating to the document 2D48. 2D48 was tendered through witness Branimir Bugarski on the 2nd December, 2008, and because of incorrect CLSS translation, 2D48 is marked for identification pending a correct translation. The correct translation was received on the 5th December and uploaded into the e-court system under the number 2D05-0312. Immediately, all parties were informed, and on 10th December, 2008, the Prosecution informed us that they accept the new translation. Therefore, the Defence asks for the admission of this exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit 2D45 [sic] will become -- admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Secondly, I would like to ask if we can go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I've just seen on page 1, line 19, I think the exhibit number is 2D48, not 45.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid, please call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ivetic will be handling the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would call Mr. Zeljko Markovic to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the time estimate, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I should be between one hour and one and a half hours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. As you know, I'm Dan Ivetic, one of the attorneys for Milan Lukic, and for purposes of the record, I would ask you to please introduce yourself briefly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Zeljko Markovic. I was born on the 15th of January, 1967, in Pljevlja in Republic of Montenegro. I'm married, father of 2. I graduated from a faculty in Belgrade and I worked for 20 years as a police officer in the Republic of Serbia MUP until I was invalided out. I worked in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and again, if you could stay close to the microphone, the translators are asking for that. You've already told us about some of the factors from your background. Could you please give us some background as to your educational history?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After I completed the secondary school in Bijela Polje in Montenegro, I went to Belgrade to study where I graduated from the faculty of mathematics and natural science. I graduated in geography, and then I specialized at the same faculty. I specialized in maritime tourism.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned that you have 20 years experience as a police officer in the Republic of Serbia MUP. I would ask you in this regard if you could enlighten us as to whether or not the MUP in Republic of Serbia in 1992 or the years leading up to it had any educational faculty or college in Obrenovac.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP of the Republic of Serbia in 1992 and before that did not have any faculty, not only in Obrenovac but in the Republic of Serbia. There was no faculty. There was just the post-secondary college in Saradusna [phoen] Street. That's where it is now, and after a while in 1992 or maybe even 2000, I'm not quite sure, a faculty of -- the security faculty was set up by the institute of security in Banica [phoen], so that was the only faculty of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia that exists, and the higher school, the post-secondary school in Zemun. There is also the secondary school in Kamenica near Novi Sad which is a MUP facility, and there is a small boarding school for police trainees in Klis near Novi Sad. Other than that, there is nothing in the Republic of Serbia. There are no secondary schools, police secondary schools in Obrenovac. There are other secondary schools, I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and I'm waiting to allow the English translation and the transcript to catch up with us, so if I have a pause, that's why it is. Now, one more question on that topic. What precise job position did you have in the year 1992 within the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I held several jobs. I first started out as a police officer, as a beat policeman in the MUP of Republic of Serbia until I graduated, so my posts changed as time went by. In 1992, I worked in the unit providing security to the republican organs of the Republic of Serbia government.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and again, I'm just waiting for the transcript. And for the complete picture, you mentioned you were subjected to an invalid pension from the MUP. Could you -- retirement or pensia. If you could tell us, are you currently employed in any other field or position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not willing, I'm not able to work because I have an injury in my leg, the right hip, to be more specific, because I was in a traffic accident. It was a serious accident. It happened in 2003, and since 2005, the 21st of June, I have been retired and I am not able to engage in any kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and if you could just tell us where you resided in the year 1992 and if you resided alone or if anyone resided with you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the time that I arrived in Belgrade when I got the job after I left the campus where I had been staying during my studies, I changed apartments several times. I rented apartments. In 1992, I lived in Zemun, in Banjicka [phoen] Street. The number is 35. I lived with my wife's grandmother, Angelina Klincov. That's the grandmother's name. My wife's name is Natasa. It was a small outhouse in the yard, and I lived there with my wife, Natasa. We've lived together since the 7th of June, 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now I'd ask you to tell us, please, if you know Milan Lukic, that is to say the gentleman sitting right behind me.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Milan Lukic very well. We met in 1987 in Studenski Grad, the halls of residence in Belgrade. When I came there to study, I lived there. Mr. Milan Lukic often came to visit the Studenski Grad facility. He didn't live there in the halls of residence, but he came to see his brother Novica, who lived in the same building where I did. And since Novica socialized with my friends from Bijela Polje and since he often came to their room, room number 38, in this building in Studenski Grad, that's how I met Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to Mr. Milan Lukic, did you have occasion to socialize with him on those occasions when he came to visit his brother Novica, and if, so how frequently and what types of activities?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Milan came to Studenski Grad quite often after we met. We soon started socializing quite extensively, not only I but also some other friends of mine, colleagues, students from Bijelo Polje who studied with me at the time, and since Milan was a football player - he was an athlete, in other words - and I used to play football, too, back in Bijelo Polje, it was easy for us to find common ground as a basis for our friendship. He was very communicative. He always had a smile on his face, and I liked it. So I socialized with him more than I did with his brother Novica. I merely knew his brother. We were acquainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if I could ask you, from the time period between 1987 until 1992, did Milan Lukic remain, remain in Belgrade that entire time period or not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stayed in Studenski Grad until 1989. That's when I got a job, in September, and that's when I left, but up until 1989, about a year, a year and a half, Milan continued coming to Studenski Grad. And after that, as far as I know, he went to Germany - at least, that's what he told me - and then to Switzerland. I would not go that often to Studenski Grad. I was not there as often as I was before, but I remember that once or twice, I saw him there in Studenski Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you -- if you could clarify for us -- waiting for the translation to catch up, but if you could clarify for us, did you see Milan Lukic after he left Yugoslavia for Europe -- to do what he was doing in Europe and in Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him. I don't know what year that was, perhaps 1989 or 1990 or thereabouts, while he was in Germany, and he told me that he played football in some league in Germany and that he was a waiter, a barman. And then our next meeting was in 1992, the one that I really remember. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that. Now, if you could describe the Milan Lukic that you knew from the days in the student city, the Milan Lukic that went to Europe, in Germany and Switzerland. How would you describe him as a person and in his interactions with other people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As a person in context with other people, I would describe him as a paragon of gentleman-like behavior, if I could use those terms. All the friends, all the students who met him were astonished and enthusiastic about him. He was -- on the one hand, he was always quiet and not pushy, but on the other hand he was friendly. He was always a modest person. He lived with modest means, and he used to sell bottles of juice for food vouchers and then he would take those to the bus station and sell them there in order to get by. But he would always invite us for a drink, although he was a student himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Again, we're just waiting for the transcript to catch up. I apologize. It's one of the nuances of this courtroom. How would you describe how Milan Lukic acted towards persons of different ethnic groups? That is to say, did he treat people differently based on what ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you a specific example. I was in room 42 in Studenski Grad. There were three roommates. There were four of us, all told. One of them was a Montenegrin, the same ethnic background as I was, and the other two were Muslims from Bijelo Polje. I can even give you the names. He knew them and he socialized them in the same way in which he did with me. I never saw any traces of intolerance in him towards any people of other ethnic backgrounds, religion, or race.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: And I can even give you the names of those students. Mersud Lakic, my roommate; he got a master's degree in molecular biology in Belgrade. Now he also has his doctoral degree in molecular biology. He lives in the United States of America. Also, Saladin Udzevic [phoen], also from Bijelo Polje. We would all hang out together, we would play various card games and we had -- we would have a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned earlier that you recalled an occasion in 1992 when you had contact with Milan Lukic who had returned from Europe to Belgrade. Can you tell us about the first such instance in 1992 that you have a recollection of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in late April or early May when he came back from Switzerland, as he told me, and I remember that he had some problems because his mother was sick. He told me that he had to take his mother from Visegrad there. I don't know how he planned to do that because it was wartime at that time there, and he didn't have any means of transportation. That was in late April, early May. I know well that I saw him in Studenski Grad on the 5th of May. I went to the photocopy office there to photocopy some books because my wife and I were students at the time and there was a photocopy office there which was cheaper, and all students used this facility. We met there, and we went to a cafe called Index, which is in the immediate vicinity of Studenski Grad. That was our custom from our student days to go there, to the Index cafe. It was nothing special, but it did have an advantage for students because all students who got the best mark in any subjects at their university would get a free hamburger and Coke, for him or her and their friends. And that's why we went there. It was just a habit. I think that there was an Albanian who was the owner of the cafe. I don't know the name. I just knew this man by sight. This cafe still exists. We sat down. It was the 5th of May in the afternoon, and he says, I don't know what to do, can you help me, can you find some vehicle that I could use to go to Visegrad and fetch my mother. And I told him, I don't have a car. In fact, I did have a car, but I crashed it. It was in Montenegro, and it was being repaired. And he said that he didn't have -- I said I didn't have anyone else to ask because nobody wanted to lend their car for such a long-distance trip. And he said -- and I said, the only thing I can do was to go to a car rental shop. I knew an owner of one of the car rental shops. It was called Tref, in Sava Centre, and I suggested to him that he should wait for me a couple of minutes in Index because I should go to my house, change into my uniform because the owner would not remember me if I didn't -- if I wasn't in uniform. He knew me because he knew that I provided security in Sava Centre where the third channel of Belgrade TV was. That was the main reason, and that's how I got to know the owner. I took a taxi. I lived close by. I went home. I put on my police uniform. I didn't even go to Index. He got out immediately. We went down to Sava Centre, to this car rental shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just back up for a second to get a full picture. You indicated this was the 5th of May. Is there a reason that this date relating to this particular instance is clear in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was about to say that. It was easy for me to remember the 5th of May because the 6th of May in Serbia and in Montenegro among the families with the name of Markovic is St. George's Day, the Markovic family patron saint's day. Every 6th of May, unless something extraordinary happens to prevent me, I go to my native Vodno near Pljevlja, where my entire family celebrates St. George's Day at my uncle's house. The custom is to celebrate in the house of the eldest brother, and since my uncle was the eldest brother in the family, we did it there. So I remember the 5th of May well because on the 6th of May I was unable to attend this celebration because I had to go elsewhere, and I'll explain that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you go back to telling us how it was that you and Mr. Milan Lukic went about obtaining an automobile for this trip to Visegrad to fetch his mother.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I started to explain. I took that taxi, put on my uniform, and when we reached students' town, he got out of that Cafe Index, and we continued towards the congress centre called Sava Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what happened when you reached the rental car company?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When we got to the congress centre, we found a girl working at the agency, a girl I didn't know particularly. We said we needed a car for a day or two to go to Visegrad, how much that would be, et cetera. She answered that she did not dare to give us a car. The owner forbade it because she had heard it was a war zone there in Bosnia, because they feared that the car would be damaged or never be returned to the owner. I asked her if she could fetch the owner, named Vlada, to talk to me. She dialed the phone. He must have been somewhere around in the congress centre, and he showed up 20 minutes later. So when the owner came, I told him the whole story. I said my friend came back from Switzerland, he would need a rental car to go to Visegrad, get his mother, drive back. There will be no problem. He'll come back with the car. He's a nice guy. The owner was not really thrilled, but at one point, Milan said, I'll leave a deposit of 1.000 Swiss francs, and then the owner changed his mind. He said, pointing to me, I'll give you the car for his sake. He's the guarantor. He knew me because I worked as a security guard there, and of course he knew I was employed with the police. So he issued the car in my name, and I was the one who eventually returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could ask you, you indicated you were in your official police uniform. How was Milan Lukic dressed that day while you were in Belgrade about to set out for Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Lukic was always in casual, sporty clothes. On that day, he was wearing a suede jacket and jeans. That suede jacket was more like a dress jacket, but it was in fact an ordinary, casual jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you describe for us what type of vehicle you ended up renting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. It was a Volkswagen Golf 2, white with a Belgrade license plate, but I can't tell you the number. I really can't tell you the number because I don't remember even my own license plate, because every time I have to pay the parking metre, I have to look again at my own license plate in order to type it into my mobile phone for the parking fee SMS message.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you, when was it that you agreed to set out with Milan, that is to say, what day had you agreed to set out with Milan for Visegrad, and did you tell your family where you were going, that you were in fact going to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that day when we took the car, it became clear that I had to go with the car because it was my responsibility. The owner released the car in my name, and Milan Lukic could not drive alone with papers in my name. And I told my family when I came back, that is, I told my wife when I came back from the congress centre that I was going, but I didn't tell her I was going to Visegrad. I told her I took the car because I was going to attend that patron saint's celebration because, because as I told her, no other transport was available. There were no other bus tickets, et cetera, so I had to take a car. Anyway, I did that to alleviate her fears because otherwise, she would be afraid if I had told her where exactly I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you set out -- first of all, what was the route that you took and the precise date and approximate time when you set out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we set out in the morning at 7 a.m., meeting outside the students' town. He was waiting for me by the traffic lights, since I didn't know exactly where he lived in the neighborhood of Bezanijska Kosa, which was very new at the time. I wasn't familiar with the layout, with the streets. It was easier to meet outside students' town. We set out at 7 a.m., and I remember we tanked up at Radnicka Street in Belgrade. We continued on the Ibar motorway via Cacak and Uzice. On the way, we made a short stop at Ovcar-Kablar Gorge, a few kilometers after Cacak in the direction of Uzicka Pozega. We stopped there for 30 minutes at a restaurant called Njegos.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We had breakfast and as I remember clearly, the restaurant is call Njegos because it serves some Montenegrin delicacies. Among them, njegusi steak, which I had for breakfast, and Milan had a light breakfast, like an omelette. He wasn't very hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, did you have an occasion to encounter any check points or roadblocks on the way from Belgrade to the administrative border with Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the territory of Serbia, there were no check points, no roadblocks at least, so we had a free passage. There were routine traffic controls, and we were stopped somewhere by Sevojno at one of them, but it was just to check the papers for the car and the driver's license, no other questions asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If I can back up a bit, you had mentioned that Milan had offered some 1.000 Swiss francs for this vehicle. What was the economic situation in 1992 in the Republic of Serbia? Perhaps if you could relate that to your own personal experiences or knowledge relating to your police salary, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can explain, because that time remains etched in my memory. The 1.000 Swiss francs were made as a deposit, not a payment, by Milan Lukic. The economic situation in 1992 and 1993 in Serbia was a real catastrophe. There was a galloping inflation, and I can give you an example because life was very hard for me at that time, so I remember it well. When I received my monthly salary, by the end of the day that entire salary could buy only one German mark, and that's what we did. I was a tenant in my apartment. My rent was 40 Deutschmark, and I could buy only one Deutschmark on payday from street dealers. The very next morning, that salary couldn't buy you a loaf of bread. That's how bad the inflation was. So 1.000 Swiss francs was a treasure, great wealth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Again, I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now, if we could turn to your recitation of the trip with Milan Lukic on the 6th of May to Visegrad. Could you tell us if anything happened at the administrative border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At the administrative border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, nothing special happened. There was a routine traffic control by Serbian policeman. There were only policemen at the check point. Of course, they checked our papers, good morning, good morning, where are you going, can we see your papers. From me, since I was in uniform, they asked also the police ID card because anybody can put on a uniform and impersonate a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Again waiting for the transcript. After crossing the administrative border, did you at that point in time encounter -- encounter any check points or roadblocks on the way from the Serbian border towards the municipality of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After we crossed the border, there were two or, rather, three check points, one just after the border at a place called Vardiste where there was an army barracks, and I noticed a lot of army personnel and policemen around there. That was the first time we were stopped. They asked where we were going, look at our documents. They also checked the boot of the car. We answered all these questions and continued. The next stop was in Dobrun where the road forks towards Lima and Visegrad. There was another check point manned by army personnel and a few policemen, the same story as in Vardiste, the same procedure, and then we continued on the way to Visegrad. The next stop was a check point, if you can call it a check point, manned only by the police, no army. I remember it very well because there's a petrol station on the left side, and the policemen were on the right side of the road. We were stopped there. We were asked where we were going. They looked at Milan's documents. I think it was a passport that he offered, and I remember one of the policemen said, you, sir, have to go to the duty service of the police station to register. When Milan asked why, they said, all will be explained to you at the duty service of SUP Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you explain for us where the police station or SUP of Visegrad was located and where you had to travel to get to it, what route you took?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we continued straight on, downhill, then the road takes you a bit to the left, and across a small bridge leading to the centre of Visegrad. When you take a slight left turn, there was a police station, and across the road there was a small green market, so we stopped on that road leading to the centre. I parked outside the police station. There were some policemen there carrying rifles, I noticed. Milan got out. I didn't want to get out because I was wearing a different uniform, and he got into the police station. The entrance was on the upper side of the building. It was a two-storey, old building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could back up a bit. Where precisely did you park? Where exactly did you park? Could you describe the location where you parked?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you take the turn towards the police station going towards the centre, if you take it further left, there was a small green market where I parked. I could not park exactly outside the police station because it's to the left of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? Did you both go into the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I stayed in the car. Milan went into the police station alone. I waited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to what incidents in the indictment is this evidence related?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the arrival of Milan Lukic to Visegrad, which is an element that's been alleged by the Prosecution. It's not an indictment charge, as this witness was presented under Rule 65 ter for explaining how it was that Milan Lukic came to Visegrad, when he came to Visegrad, and we're getting up to the critical part now. I don't want to taint the witness, but we're getting to the critical part of why he remained in Visegrad and what he was doing there at the beginning of the war. So it's not a crime yet. The witness is also an alibi witness to a specific time period later that we'll be getting to that will be of interest to two of the counts in the indictment against him. At this point in time, we're still explaining, presenting for the first time the true and accurate picture of how Milan Lukic came to Visegrad, which has been so often the subject of the Prosecution's various witnesses who claim to have seen him there earlier or claim to see him there under different circumstances, so it's of critical importance, and this is the only witness we are presenting for -- for that time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Markovic, you have indicated that Milan went into the police station alone and you waited. What happened then? How long was Mr. Lukic in the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he stayed quite a while, 45 minutes or so. I got tired of waiting, I remember, and I was wondering why he was taking so long. And then he showed up, dressed in a police uniform, with a belt on him but no weapons. I remember that because I started laughing when I saw him wearing a police uniform because he was wearing pants that ended 20 centimetres above his shoes. They must have been out of larger sizes. He got out together with three other policemen. I got out of the car to see what it was all about, and I said, laughing, what is this story? And he answered, I have to stay. They mobilized me into the reserve force of the police. And I said, how come? What are you going to do about your mother? And he said, I have to stay. It not going to be that bad. I'll be in the escort of -- in the security detail of Commander Tomic. I don't know this Tomic, but there are many Tomices in my native place of Vrulja, and I remember thinking that it's strange that there is a Tomic in Visegrad as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what -- what, if anything, happened at that time? What did you do at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what to do, and I asked him, what are we going to do now? Shall I go fetch your mother? Where does she live? And he said, well, you can't go, you don't know where she lives. And although we were laughing about those short trousers, I could see that he was rather upset, and he said, I'm very sorry about this, brother, you just go on your way. And the other policemen told me, get into the car, sir. We'll escort you up to Vardiste. You go on your way, and he has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you then at that point in time return from whence you had came, and did you have occasion to return the rental vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two policemen got into a Lada Niva vehicle with the police registration plates. Milan got back into the police station with another policeman, so two policemen drove ahead of me. I followed in my Golf, and nobody checked me anymore at the check points because the policeman ahead explained obviously something to the crew at the check points. They took me up to Vardiste, and from then on I returned to Belgrade. I drove back the vehicle the next day to the owner, Vlada Tref.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when is the next time that you have a clear recollection of being in contact with Milan Lukic after this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: So he stayed in Bosnia, and after that, the next time was not much later. It was the 7th of June, and I was astonished to get his call. He called me at my home, 613506. Now they added another 3 in front of the 6, my flat in Zemun. I was dining with my very close friends from Novi Sad because every year, and you remember I said I've lived together with my wife since the 7th of June, 1988, and we always celebrate our own anniversary either at home or at a restaurant or with my best men in Novi Sad, and I know that it was the 7th of June because he called me that evening, and I didn't go to see him because, as I said, it was this anniversary dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that it was -- to clear up the transcript, I think in the translation it came through that it was a good friend that was with you and your wife for this anniversary dinner. Who exactly was this friend, and what was his precise relationship with you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a good friend, but in fact he's what we call my kum, my best man at my wedding, and his wife from Novi Sad. His name is Darko Boskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So he's your kum or godbrother. Now, did Milan Lukic indicate where he was calling from, and did you make any plans with Milan Lukic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He called me. I don't know from which number. Those are very old exchanges, and to this day you cannot get call identification. It took a while to get through because the call first comes to the main house where the grandma lives and then to my outhouse. Anyway, he said he came on a short visit because of his mother and that I should see him in that cafe called 10 where we usually met, Index 10. But I couldn't go, unfortunately, because I had this anniversary dinner with my best man and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you make arrangements with Mr. Lukic to meet him at some other time, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I even invited him to join us. He actually was reluctant to call on me at my house because he didn't want to be in the way. I do that myself. I prefer to meet with my friends in cafes and restaurants. I said, anyway, that I couldn't see him at all on the 7th, and I said that instead, the next morning on the 8th I would come to the students' town at 10.00 in the morning. And anyway, I had to go there to the library to return some books. So we set a date for the next day at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the location where you agreed or arranged to meet Mr. Lukic, what was that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That cafe was Index in students' town, because that was the shortest way, and it was our usual meeting place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have any other appointments that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After Milan I had another meeting at half past 10, and that's why I suggested to Milan that we should meet at 10, because the previous day I got a call from my uncle, Sava Lekovic, who lived in Mustanica. It's a suburb, some 20 or 30 kilometers away from Belgrade itself. He was supposed to come to Belgrade, and I was supposed to accompany him to look for a rental apartment in Belgrade for him. So I arranged with my uncle to meet at half past 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you actually go ahead and have the meeting with Milan Lukic at 10.00 on the 8th of June, 1992, in the Cafe Index in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I arrived, Milan was already there in Cafe Index and he was drinking a Coke. We met but very briefly. He was in a big hurry, and I asked him how he was, what he was doing, and the only answer I got was, leave me be, I'm very tense. If it hadn't been for my mother, I would never have returned. I could have stayed in Switzerland. He was very tense, and he explained to me that he was in a hurry because he had brought his mother to Belgrade for a medical check-up. She was ill, and one of the questions -- one of the reasons why he actually called me was this: He says, I have some Muslims in my apartment, some friends of mine from Visegrad or from wherever, I don't know that, and I'm supposed to take them to Novi Pazar. What's the situation en route to Novi Pazar? Is it safe?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your response to this inquiry by Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a strange question. I told him that there were no problems for people in the Republic of Serbia, regardless of their religious affiliation. They would have no problems going to Novi Pazar. Nobody would ask them any questions. There could be some routine traffic stops by the police, but if -- and I said, if you need me, I'll accompany you, but there's no need, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long did this encounter with Milan Lukic last at the Cafe Index in the students' city in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. When my uncle arrived, Milan was not there. It was less than half an hour, just ten minutes or so. He was in a hurry, probably because of his mother. He had to go to the hospital, so it was about 15, 20 minutes. By the time my uncle arrived at half past 10, he was already gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you have occasion to speak with Milan Lukic in the days following this meeting or encounter with him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your question. I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After this meeting with Mr. Lukic on the 8th of June, 1992, did you have occasion to speak with him again in the following days?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, that was the 9th - on the 8th we met. On the 9th, he did not call, and I found it strange. I wanted to know what was happening, so he called me on the 10th. The day after our meeting, he didn't call. He called on the day after that, which was the 10th, and he told me that he would wrap up himself and that he would go to Novi Pazar. Thank you, we'll see each other. And I said to him, have a safe trip, and that was just a brief conversation. I didn't want to speak to him long over the phone because I had this courtesy phone. There were other tenants there. I didn't want to keep the line occupied for a long time, so I always spoke to people very briefly. They didn't -- people actually avoid calling me because my grandmother was old and it was a big hassle for her to switch the phone over to my phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, after that point in time, did you have any further contact with Mr. Milan Lukic during the duration of the Bosnian civil war, that is to say, the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: During the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I did not have any encounters with him, no phone calls. I don't know where he was, what was happening. The first meeting with Milan Lukic that I had after the end of the war was in late 1996 or 1997, something like that, and this is how it happened. At that time, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, vehicles were imported from western Europe. So all citizens of Serbia and Montenegro would go to Bosnia to buy vehicles because those vehicles were the only ones that could be transferred to Belgrade plates and other plates issued in the Republic of Serbia. And that's how I, like all the other citizens, went to Visegrad, it was a free territory, to buy a car, and I saw Milan in Visegrad because he put me in touch with some of his friends, acquaintances, and he showed me several cars, and I did buy one of those cars. That was the first time that I saw him in the town of Visegrad, which looked like there never was a war. I never saw any damage to any houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, did you have any other contact with Mr. Lukic during that time period, during the 1990s, after the war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After the war, apart from what I've just told you, this contact that I had with him about the purchase of the car, I didn't have any other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I pass the witness to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Dermot Groome. I represent the Prosecution, and I'll be asking you some questions here this morning.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Pleased to meet you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a few questions to begin with respect to your background. You said that you studied maritime tourism and that you also attended the faculty of math and sciences. Did you ever receive a degree from the faculty?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me correct you. At the faculty of math and sciences, I graduated in geography, and geography includes a course in maritime or coastal tourism. This is what I studied as a post-graduate student, and this is what I specialized. It is a post-graduate degree, which is lower than the master's degree. Of course, I graduated from the faculty, and then I further specialized, and my average mark was 9 out of 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you a few questions about your service as a police officer, and if I could begin with 1992. Your testimony here today was that when you received your monthly salary that it could only be converted to 1 Deutschmark, and it was insufficient to buy a loaf of bread the following day, and it also seems that it was insufficient to pay your rent of 40 Deutschmarks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult. It was very difficult to pay the rent. I had to do some work privately, to chop wood, to do some painting jobs, as much as I could to make ends meet for my family. I also got some assistance from my father who lived in the countryside, meat, dairy products, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you've told us what you'd done up until 1992. What year did you retire from the police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I believe you said that you retired because of an injury you received in a car accident. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when was that car accident?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The accident was on the 28th of December, 2003, at the corner of Mokroluska and Vojaslavalica [phoen] Street in the morning hours, 6.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you just to summarize briefly, what types of positions did you have in the police between 1992 and your retirement in 2005?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if counsel's got something specific, but I would object to relevance at this point, and it's beyond the scope of the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, what's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, surely his professional career and educational background would be matters that would be relevant to his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, again just briefly, if you could tell us the different positions that you held and the type of work you did as a police officer between 1992 and 2005 when you retired.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a problem. I changed a number of posts and let me take them one by one. I started in the Novi Belgrade, New Belgrade police station as a beat policeman where I covered various sectors, depending on the requirements of the service. I provided security at the Stari Merkator, the Sava Centre, congress centre, the students' town, and I also performed other duties. It's sectoral work. It's similar to patrols where you patrol the whole of New Belgrade. That's how it was at the time. In 1991, I was transferred from the New Belgrade police station to the Ministry of the Interior. This is the republican SUP of the Republic of Serbia, in Kneza Milosa Street. At the beginning, I provided security to republican organs and persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not so important that we have the specific places that you provided security, but it seems that for most of your police career, you were engaged in providing security for -- to whomever you were assigned to protect. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I merely started telling you all this in detail, but I can cut to the chase. So from a beat officer in New Belgrade, I moved to MUP where I provided security to the National Assembly in Belgrade, the building itself, and then after I completed my studies, I move to the city Secretariat of the Interior where I worked as a plain-clothes inspector in the sector for public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And as a plain-clothes officer, did you have any particular type of crime that you were engaged in investigating?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not investigate crimes. We dealt with public law and order, and in our sector, in the Belgrade SUP, that had to do with violent conduct, gambling, and prostitution. So these were the tasks that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, since your retirement, we've heard that you receive a disability pension. Aside from that disability pension, do you do anything presently to earn income?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, and I couldn't do any work physically, and I also don't have the right to work. My wife works. She also has a university degree, and we are able to live a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know a cafe by the name of Cafe Bellissimo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Belgrade very well, and I know that cafe Bellissimo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that a cafe that have you any ownership interest in?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I don't know why you're asking me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to speak to you a bit about your relationship with Milan Lukic. Is it fair to say that have you known Milan Lukic for approximately 20 years?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I've told you, I've known him since 1987, October 1987, in fact. We came to students' town in end October, and I've known him all the time since, but we didn't see each other every day. We each had our own lives. We did see each other often while he was in Belgrade over a year, a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that would make it 21 years that you've known Milan Lukic, correct? 1987 to 2008?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you consider yourself a very close friend of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time when we met at students' town, we were good friends. I was not his only friend. He had other friends, but we were good friends as students. However, in time our meetings became rarer. After he left students' town, you can count on the fingers of one hand the times we met. You cannot consider somebody a very close friend if you don't see them for 15 years. You can't call a close friend anyone whom you don't see and visit at home fairly regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And sir, you said that you cannot consider someone a close friend if you don't see them for 15 years. Is there a 15-year period in your relationship with Mr. Milan Lukic that you did not see him? Yes or no, if you can answer it with yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understood that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the statement -- the transcript records you as saying: "You cannot consider somebody a very close friend if you don't see them for 15 years." So what I'm asking you, when you said that, was that a reference to Milan Lukic? Was there a period of time that you had not seen him for 15 years?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you when I saw him last. Now I would have to count -- well, you can read in my statement when I saw him last.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to do any mathematics in your head. When is the most recent time that you have seen Milan Lukic? When have you most recently seen him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The last time, it was in Visegrad when I bought the car. That was the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what year was that again, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 1996 or early 1997 when it was possible to import cars from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So between that time and the time that you looked across the courtroom and saw him here today, you had not seen Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see him from that time until today, so from the time when I bought the car in 1996 or 1997, I had not seen him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you speak with him during that time period?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulty recognizing him here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he's changed. He's put on quite a lot of weight, and his hair is shorter. His hair used to be much longer, but the face remained the same. I was able to recognize him, although he's now much heavier. As a student, he had longer hair, especially in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at transcript 10, line 19, when speaking about Djurdjevdan day, which seems to be why you remember this early May encounter, you said that you remember that Djurdjevdan day, it's expected that you would spend it with your family unless something extraordinary happens. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and I also stressed that I mostly went to Pljevlja for St. George's Day to attend the feast which was at that time organised by my uncle as the eldest brother in the family, unless something else happened. It's a long way away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: And I sometimes prefer not to go because there were some other events, but I would always have at least a mini-feast in my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, can I take it as an indication of the depth of the relationship you had with Milan Lukic in 1992 that you did not attend this important family celebration but instead made a decision to help Milan Lukic that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't mean that it was a deep relationship, but if a man, if a friend, your neighbor, your relative, tells you that they had some health problems, it's a humanitarian reason and it's a much stronger reason than some feast because I was not the only family member there. Somebody did come to represent my family in my uncle's house, my father, my sister. But since his mother was sick, I agreed, and I would not have gone there had it been possible for him to get a car on his own. There would have been no need for me to go there, but I had to bring the vehicle back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going first now to -- well, let me ask you this. Mr. Ivetic said in explaining the purpose of your testimony, one of the purposes of your testimony, said, and this is transcript page 17, line 15: "We're still explaining -- presenting for the first time the true and accurate picture of how Milan Lukic came to Visegrad, which has been so often the subject of Prosecution's various witnesses who claim to have seen him there earlier." Is it your evidence that when you went with Mr. Lukic, Milan Lukic, to Visegrad on the 6th of May, that this was the first time that he was returning to Visegrad after his time in Germany and Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Whether Milan had gone to Visegrad before? Well, I don't know that. I only can say that he went there with me on that day and that he remained in the territory of Visegrad as I described it. Now, as to whether he had been to the territory of Visegrad before, I can't tell you. He may have, but I can't tell you. He had just got back from Switzerland, and why would he have gone to Bosnia at all unless he was hard-pressed to do so. I don't know that, at any rate. I do know that he remained there on that day when he went with me, and I can't tell you things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you describe having numerous conversations can him. At this -- during this period of time, did he ever say to you, hey, I've been in Bosnia, there's a war going on? Had he ever discussed with you having been in Bosnia prior to the date that you took him there but after he returned from Europe?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't discuss that with me when he came. I told you that I saw him only briefly after he moved abroad. I remained in the students' town, and in that period I only saw him very seldom. We didn't talked about the war in Bosnia. We talked about our lives, girls, football, mostly football. I love football. I can talk about football all day long, and he liked the topic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But the fact is, you have no recollection of him saying to you, I've been in Bosnia and I'm asking you to help me return to Bosnia, at the time he asked you for assistance in finding a car?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that. We didn't talk about that. I don't think that he was because he had just come back from Switzerland. He didn't tell me about having gone to Bosnia. We did not discuss this topic at all. The only topic that related to his departure for Bosnia had to do with his mother's illness. We did not talk about this. We talked about some casual private affairs of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your belief that the time that you traveled with him to Bosnia is the first time that he was returning to Visegrad since he had been in Europe?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina broke out. I really don't know the exact date. When he went abroad, that was a year and a half while we were in the students' hall, he didn't go to Bosnia. I met him once. I don't know whether he went to Bosnia or not. I don't know when the war started. As regards the war in Bosnia, we didn't talk about that at all. I didn't ask him any questions. He didn't tell me anything. I don't know that. I think he didn't, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the breakout of war in Bosnia was a rather significant event that was covered in the international media, not simply, I would imagine, the Yugoslav media. Are you able to say when the war in Bosnia started?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. As far as I can recall, the war first broke out in Slovenia, then the Croatia, then in Krajina, then in Bosnia. There were so many of those events, and I really don't know. I can't recall. I don't want to remember. I don't like war. I like it when people are able to live normally, so I really don't know when the war broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and most of its parts. I don't know where -- when the war broke out. I had my own tasks, my own jobs, I had my private problems, and so on. I had other stuff to think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you tell me a year?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when it began. I don't know when it ended. I think it ended about 1995, 1996, something like that. I don't remember those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to embark on an entirely new area. I'm not sure when the Chamber was planning on taking a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, you testified that you did not recall the year the war started, and I must put it to you plainly: The implausibility of you recalling that Milan Lukic had a glass of Coke and was wearing a suede jacket on the 8th of June 16 years ago and yet be unable to recall when war broke out in your country. Do you not agree that this is rather implausible, that you have such detailed memory about a fact that most of us would forget but have no recollection about the year in which the war broke out in your country?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. Asked and answered. Sorry. Waiting for the translation. I would object, asked and answered, and I believe at this point counsel is making arguments, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I believe the question is perfectly proper, Mr. Ivetic. Perfectly proper. I see nothing wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand what question I'm putting to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand very well. I remember the jacket he wore because he used to wear it when he was a student at the students' town, this suede jacket, and as for the beginning of the war in the then-Yugoslavia, how can I know the date? I lived in Serbia where there was no war. The war broke out in the territory of Slovenia and Croatia and Bosnia. I remember the war. I just don't know the date. After the Zvezda-Dinamo match in Zagreb when the supporters of Zvezda barely got out of there alive, of course I remember there was a war on. And then soon afterwards, the war in Bosnia began, but I don't remember the date. I didn't lead the army to remember the date. I was engaged in different work. I worked in MUP as a security man. The war in the territory of a country outside of Serbia was not really my business.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to have a very specific memory about this very infamous football match that took place in Zagreb. What was the date of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I know that it was at the Dinamo stadium in Zagreb and that Boban hit somebody there. You can see that video clip sometimes on TV still today. I told you, I played football in the veterans' club.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't challenge your memory about what happened. What I'm ask you is, as you sit here today, you do not know the date of that football match, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I know it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you refer to the war taking place in Slovenia and what are now different countries, at the time the war broke out, it was one country, Yugoslavia, your country. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the war began in Slovenia, and at that time Yugoslavia still existed. It was still one country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you were a police officer in that country in which a war broke out, and you are unable to even tell me the year that the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a police officer, but of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and I really don't know what was going on in Slovenia. I can't remember all that. The army was involved in the war, or whoever. I can't answer these questions. I was not in the army, and I was not in those regions. Perhaps I went through Slovenia once in passing. I can't tell you things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you've explained to us why you remember the suede jacket. What was so memorable about the can of Coca-Cola that Mr. Lukic had that now 16 years on you have a specific memory of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a can of Coca-Cola, but he was always drinking Coke. He arrived to that establishment before I did, and he had already ordered a drink and he always drank Coke. That was something I remember. Sometimes he went to McDonald's in Belgrade where he sometimes had a hamburger, but he always had a Coke, inevitably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your statement on page 2, you state: "We met briefly for a drink the following morning. We could not stay long because Milan was in a hurry. He told me he had some Muslim friends in his flat in Belgrade and that his mother was due for medical check-ups." Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you recall that he told you that he had some Muslims who were his friends living in his apartment in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, and I understood that's the reason why he called me, to ask me about taking those Muslims to Novi Pazar. I don't know whether they were from Visegrad or some other town in Bosnia. In fact, he asked me if they would be safe going to Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your recollection is that he was describing Muslim friends from Bosnia. It may have been Visegrad, or it may have been some other place in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They must have been good friends if he was allowing them to stay at his apartment with him not there, with him being with you, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably knew one another well. He came to Belgrade for his mother, and he asked me about taking them to Novi Pazar. They must have been good friends if they lived in his apartment, but you have to ask him. I cannot tell you whether they were friends or not or how good friends because I never saw these people. I don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: All I'm interested from you, sir, is what you know from your personal knowledge or what he may have said to you. So if you don't know, please just explain that, and I'll ask you another question. Now, you've testified that he wanted to bring his mother to get some medical check-ups. Did he tell you where his mother was having these medical check-ups?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not tell me that. He just told me he was in a hurry because he had to make it to the medical appointment. I didn't ask him which hospital. I thought it was superfluous to ask. He took her to the doctor. Where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So from what you're saying now, it seems the medical appointment was on the 8th of June. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You see, what things are like in the health system of the Republic of Serbia, somebody from Bosnia or Montenegro would get a referral where they live and would travel to Belgrade with that referral. I don't know what it says, but the referral doesn't say, see the doctor on such and such a date. I don't know if his mother had a referral or which hospital she was supposed to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you met him the morning of the 8th of June, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you just testified that - I'm quoting you - "He just told me that he was in a hurry because he had to make it to the medical appointment." That suggests to me that on the day he was meeting you, his mother had an appointment scheduled and he need to leave you quickly to bring her there. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he told me he was taking his mother there, that he was in a rush, and that some Muslims were living in his apartment. I asked him, what are you doing? He said, nothing much, I'm in a hurry, and I understood the reason he wanted to see me was to ask me about the safety of those Muslims in his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, being a good friend, did you say to him, what's wrong with your mother, is there anything I can do to help? Did you inquire about his mother's health?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked what it was about. He said, she's in a bad way. He found some acquaintance of an acquaintance who is a doctor. He was taking her there. I didn't ask anymore because I'm not a medical man myself. I had no acquaintances in hospitals, and I assumed he already knew who he was going to see. I asked her what condition she's in. She said -- he said, not good, she's ill, she's old, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he say specifically what illness she had or what her ailment was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he tell you the nature of the check-up she was scheduled to have?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't talk about details. The entire conversation about his mother was that he brought his mother there, that that's why he was there, he was in a hurry because of her, and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No need to repeat. If you could answer my question in a yes or no, I would appreciate that. Did his parents ever come to live in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you that his parents had moved in with him and were living with him in his apartment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either. We did not visit each other at home. We usually met outside, in town, at Cafe Index 10, in students' town while he was there, sometimes at McDonald's, we played football together, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, on page 1, paragraph 6, of your statement, you say: "He," meaning Milan Lukic, "he told me that he had to go to Visegrad to take his parents out of the war zone." Is that an accurate reflection or statement of what you told the Defence team that was recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can -- it's more of a way of a suggestion rather than an objection, but if you're going to quote something, it'd be good to quote the original Serbian rather than the translation of the English which gets retranslated into Serbian and it will perhaps provide the witness with a copy of the Serbian original document which you're referring, to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not speaking Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you want him to do? He doesn't speak Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have an original document in Serbian. He's using the English translation. If he's going to use an exhibit, present it to the witness. It's the witness's own statement. He's doing something -- put it on the screen, put it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put it on the screen or on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour. It seems to me the more appropriate course would be if the witness says he needs it, then certainly, but it seems that if he says I remember I said that, then what's the point of putting up a statement? So I'd ask that he be allowed to answer whether he remembers saying that, and if he doesn't, then I'll make attempts to get the statement before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have the statement before him in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 1D 220094 be called up on the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, there's a screen in front of you. I believe it's going to be the screen on your right-hand side. There will be a copy of the statement that you gave to the Defence. I'm going to ask -- that's also 65 ter number 26. If you need to refer to that, if your recollection is not clear about your statement, then by all means, please look at that. Now, sir, let me ask my question again. On page 1, the sixth paragraph, you state: "He told me that he had to go to Visegrad to take his parents out of the war zone." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did he ever do that? Did he ever bring his parents out of the war zone into Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That day when I went with him, he did not do that because he stayed in Visegrad. As for the date mentioned, the 9th or the 8th of June when I saw him in Cafe Index 10, he told me he had brought his mother. I didn't see her. I don't know whether he managed to bring his parents over, but he told me on that date that he had brought his mother for a medical check-up and that he was in a hurry for that medical check-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the trip that you made down there that you did not go to your family celebration, you rented a car, you drove it down there, the purpose of that trip was for him to bring his parents back out of the war zone, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of that journey was for him to bring back his mother who was ill or his parents, both, and I traveled with him because he was unable to rent a car himself. I had to rent it for him, and I had to bring the car back. Otherwise, he would have gone alone. But since I was the guarantor for the car, I traveled with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now you've testified that he wasn't allowed to return. So my question to you is, why didn't you just bring his parents back? You're there. You're with a car. You're driving back to Belgrade. Why didn't you bring his parents back to Belgrade out of the war zone?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Here is the answer to your question. When he emerged from the police station in uniform, I asked him, should I go fetch your mother? He said no. I didn't know where that village was. The war was already going on. I didn't know which parts. I didn't know whether the army was present or not, and I couldn't go to his village if I didn't know where it was. I would have gone if he could have arranged it. However, the policemen told me immediately to get back into my car and that they would escort me out, and they took him away. I don't know what for and where, and they took me back to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now you've said that one of the purposes of the trip was to bring his mother up to Belgrade because of her health. That's the 6th of May. It's also your evidence that he did not bring his mother up because of medical reasons until the beginning of June, about a month later, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He was going to bring her, and that's why we rented a car, and he told me in June that he had brought his mother on the 8th. On the 8th, I didn't see her, but he told me he had brought his mother the evening before when he gave me a call.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about something you said in direct examination. The transcript at page 16, line 15, records you as saying, and this is the point in time where you're describing what happens when you arrive at the police station in Visegrad. Now, the transcript records you as saying: "I didn't want to get out because I was wearing a different uniform." Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for me to go into the police station. I was wearing the uniform of the Republic of Serbia. There was no need for me to go into the police station because only he was summoned, not I. I was waiting in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you appreciate that it's different to say there was no need to go into the police station. From what you said earlier here today, "I didn't want to get out..." meaning get out of your car "... because I was wearing a different uniform." What might have happened had you gotten out of the car wearing a police uniform from the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing special would have happened, but I was wearing the uniform of the Republic of Serbia, and there was no need for me to go in. Nothing bad would have happened. They have would have asked me who I was, where I was going. In fact, as it turned out they were rather kind and decent to me. They even gave me an escort back, and he was the only one who was summoned to the duty service of the SUP, not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, Milan Lukic has previously stated in statements that he received training prior to returning to Visegrad. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the 7th of June, you say that you had dinner with your kum. For those of us non-Serbs, am I correct in saying that the kum relationship is one of the strongest bonds that can exist between two Serbian men?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the kum relationship is a good, fair relationship in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If your kum were called to testify before this Tribunal about that dinner that you had on the 7th of June, is there any possibility in your mind that he might be mistaken about who he had dinner with that night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he would be mistaken for a moment because he remembers the date. Every year he brings a present to me and my wife. It's the best friend I have of all times. I went to primary and secondary school with him, and he lives in Novi Sad. It's a really deep, good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the conversation you had with Milan Lukic when he's asking your advice about how safe it might be to bring his Muslim friends to Novi Pazar. And the question that I have for you -- well, first let me ask you, is there an area in Serbia that actually has a significant Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, there are Muslims in Visegrad, and otherwise, there are Muslims in the Raska district in Tutin and Sjenica and Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about Sandzak area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Right, right. I omitted that. Part of Sandzak encompasses Tutin. Sandzak also covers a part of Montenegro, Pljevlja, Sjenica, Visegrad, and Gorazde, as well, as well as some towns in Serbia like Tutin and Sjenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I correct in saying that the Sandzak area, the part that is in Serbia, has a significant Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where is Novi Pazar in relation to Sandzak, the Sandzak area? Would it be considered part of the Sandzak area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How far away --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The Raska district, yes. From Belgrade, it's 300 kilometers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How far from the Sandzak area is Novi Pazar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't tell you precisely. I don't have a map before me. I was never really that interested to measure how far Sandzak stretches in the territory of Serbia. It's like the Pester Plateau, like Backa, like Banat regions. I had never any reason to look closely at Sandzak and measure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you received your geography degree, did you study the geography of your own country, or was it of other lands?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The entire world geography.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it's your evidence that once Milan Lukic arrived in Belgrade, he called you up and asked you whether it would be safe to take Muslims down to Novi Pazar in Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he never called you from Visegrad to ask you, is it safe to transport Muslims through Serbia to get from Visegrad to Belgrade, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That night after he remained in the Visegrad police station, he did not contact me. The first time that he contacted me, well, I don't know where it was from because I don't have caller ID. He asked me if we could meet at the students' town. I did not accept that because I had other obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it's your understanding that he called you after he arrived in Belgrade on the night of 7th, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Not on the 27th. It was on the 7th in the evening for us to meet. We didn't meet then. I don't know when he had arrived in Belgrade.
