He merely call me then, and I even don't know where he called me from. He called me at my home phone, asking me if we could meet there in Belgrade. I don't know what phone number he called me from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But sir, my next question to you is, am I not correct in saying that the distance from the Bosnian border -- if a person was traveling from Visegrad to Belgrade, the distance from the Bosnian border to Belgrade is about the same distance in Serbia as it would be from Belgrade to Novi Pazar?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. Something like that. I never measure the mileage. I only know how long it takes me to get to Pljevlja because I go there to visit my father, 367 kilometers. Now, as to Novi Pazar, I really can't tell you. I went there twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, how many hours did it take you to drive from Belgrade to the Bosnian border when you were driving to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the drive to Visegrad when we went there, it took us about five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And yet, he didn't ask you your advice on that 5-hour trip with Muslims through Serbia. It was only a request made with respect to the trip between Belgrade and Novi Pazar, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Misstates the testimony. He said five hours from Belgrade to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I have, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add, you asked me about our drive to Visegrad. That's five hours, but we stopped at the Ovcar-Kablar Gorge. It depends on the car and the driver. You can take less. If I drive alone, it's a great road, and you can drive there in three and a half hours. It's a 300-kilometer trip. It depends on the car and on the driver and on the way you drive, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is it your evidence that the shortest amount of time it would take to get from Belgrade to Visegrad is three and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Three and a half, four hours, if you have a good car, I think you can do it. But if you take breaks, then it's a different story. I sometimes take seven hours instead of four hours to do a drive if I stop, if I'm not in a hurry, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But going back to my original question to you, Milan Lukic didn't call you about whether it was safe to bring Muslims from Visegrad to Belgrade but only from Belgrade to Novi Pazar, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that Muslims were in the apartment, and he asked me whether it was safe to take them to Novi Pazar. He didn't ask me anything of the sort. He merely said that they were in his apartment and that -- and asked me whether it was safe to go there to Novi Pazar, and I said that it was absolutely safe for them in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you how it was you came to testify in this case. Who first contacted you about testifying in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an answer right away. From the Defence team of Milan Lukic, it was Mr. Mihailo Lakcevic, an attorney at law. He asked me whether I would be prepared to make a statement about some circumstances that I recall that involve Milan Lukic from the student days and about our encounters. And I said it was not a problem, but I did not know much about that. I did not know much about him because it was a brief period of time and we hadn't met since, and I really don't know anything about him apart from what -- apart from what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who first mentioned the dates, June 7th, June 8th, June 10th? Who first mentioned those dates, you or Mr. Lakcevic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lakcevic did not mention any dates in the course of our conversation. He asked me, do you know him, how do you know him, from what area, and I told him, I knew him from when he came back from Switzerland, I knew the date when we drove down there because of St. George's Day, because it's a big feast. And I remember that other day when he called me, and I found it peculiar that he managed to take his mother away from the war zone. I was happy about that. Lakcevic did not ask me anything. He did not mention any dates. He merely asked me what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If he didn't mention any dates, what was said that made you realize, oh, June 7th, I got the call, June 8th, we met, June 9th, I know what I did, I know what he did, June 10th. What did Mr. Lakcevic say that made you realize that you remembered something that happened on the 7th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the dates when I saw him, up until the end of the war, up until the time when I went there to get the car, I didn't know what was going on with him. I remember this because those dates are very striking, and they stuck in my mind. I knew that I went to Bosnia to take the car and I know that it was the 7th when I had this celebration with my wife, and I didn't want to see him, although I felt sorry for him because he had come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is it your evidence that you were simply asked, when did you see Milan Lukic in 1992, and it was you that said, well, I saw him on the 6th of May and I saw him on the 8th of June. It was you that volunteered the dates.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Lakcevic asked me. He told me that he was a lawyer on the Defence team, and he asked me what I knew about him: Did you socialize with him, to what extent? And the only thing I recall was this: This was a striking thing. He went there, and I felt sorry for him for having to stay there, and he was in a bad way, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we'll move quicker if you don't repeat evidence you've already given. I'm just interested in, who's the first person who mentioned a date? And it seems that your evidence is that you are the first person to mention a date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the dates because I knew them. Lakcevic didn't know when it was that I saw them. Of course it was those dates. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to a different area. You have testified as to Milan Lukic's good character, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge of him from our student days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've stated on direct examination, pages 7 and 8, that he's a paragon of gentlemanly behavior and that you never saw any trace of intolerance in him. Am I correctly summarizing your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that he is not the type of person who is capable of committing the crimes for which he's charged?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at him from the student days, from what I knew about him from Studenski Grad, I could not imagine that he did that. I only know that he is indicted from the news media. I really don't know anything about the charges, but from based on what I know about him from our student days, he did not look like a person who could do that. I have no internet, no computer, although it may sound strange to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to challenge your assessment of his character, and I want to do it first with an exhibit that is now in evidence as P 148, and it is notes taken by a Serbian official during an interview of Milan Lukic on the 26th of October, 1992. Those notes record Milan Lukic as stating: "I personally liquidated many Muslims."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness -- this is an improper question. Where's the foundation for this witness knowing about the statements that are alleged to have been made to the police individual? It relates to a time period he says he doesn't know Milan Lukic. I don't understand what the Prosecution thinks they can obtain from this witness by presenting what they claim to be Milan Lukic's words to him. It's a matter that we have objected to in the past and we'll continue to object to as to that alleged statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you have put his character in issue, and I understand the Prosecutor to be putting this statement to the witness in that regard. Proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not suggesting that you knew what he said to the Serbian official. What I am suggesting to you that -- is had you known, had you been aware that he said this in October 1992, you would not be sitting here today attesting to his character. Is that correct, or would you still maintain that he has -- a man of good character?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I've told you that I'm speaking about his character up to 1989. That was the time when I knew him, at the time when we were at the students' town. When he left for Germany, when he left for Bosnia, we didn't socialize, so I didn't know what kind of a person he was at that time. If he had been such a person, I would never have come here to testify, and I have to say that it is my honour and my obligation to provide you with some dates that I'm aware of. I'm just telling you about his character, his honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to put one more excerpt before you, and this is an excerpt that appeared in a popular Serbian magazine named Duga during this time period in which Milan Lukic gave an interview. Are you familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're on your feet, so I'm asking you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm was going to wait for the question to be answered. I just want to make sure that I have an opportunity to object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the news magazine, Duga, a popular magazine in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object. We're bringing up the Duga article again. We've objected to this in the past. It is a -- if they're going to be relying on this document, which I think they are since it's listed as a document they want to use for cross-examine with this witness, I think I have to object. The purported interview, we don't know what date it was published, we don't have an official publication of it. We have the article that shifts from first person to third person, et cetera. It's a document that even the Prosecution as recently as a few weeks ago brought some question about when we raised it in relation to something else, so I think it's an improper document. This particular questions by itself is innocuous, but if it goes towards establishing some basis for trying to bring in the Duga article as an exhibit in this case from which the truth of the matter asserted therein is supposed to be determined, I would strenuously object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We haven't heard the question yet. What's the question in relation to the Duga?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to show the witness the article. I have both the original B/C/S as well as the translation, and I want to draw his attention to a quote -- a purported quote of Milan Lukic and then ask him whether this affects his assessment of Mr. Lukic's character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that ERN 06357586, 0635790.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you will see on the screen in front of you an article published in Duga magazine. I'm going to ask that the English -- the excerpt that I want to refer to is from page 9 of the English translation, and on the B/C/S original, I would ask that we go to the page that has page 77 at the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, who is the article by?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a second, Your Honour. Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On that point, Your Honour, I would also add to the objection that this is essentially having the Prosecution do what we were not allowed to, which is to use statements authored by third parties, presenting them to witnesses and having them testify as to it. That's precisely what we were told not to do with signed sworn statements, not newspapers articles, so I would object as to fair play and equity of arms and the manner in which we had to proceed in our case, that the same rules ought to be applied to the Prosecution as a way of trying to go around the Court's prior rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're really mixing apples and oranges here. This is not attempting to introduce a statement of a third party. It's putting to the witness a published media article which challenges his assessment that Mr. Milan Lukic is the person of a type of character that is incapable of committing the crimes with which he's charged. It's perfectly proper for me to test the accuracy of his knowledge of his general reputation in the community and with respect to that, this is an article, we don't know the exact date. We are investigating that, but it was published contemporaneously with these events, and it has quotes of Milan Lukic that were widely distributed among the public in Serbia. And I'm sorry, Your Honour, it was written by a person by the name of Radislav Matic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And published in what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The name of that magazine is Duga. It's an equivalent to Time magazine or Newsweek magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, we completely join the objections of Defence for the co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, I don't know how they can claim it was done contemporaneously when they don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me see the statement this is attributed to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that with respect to the B/C/S, it's the third column, the right-hand column, and it's in the bottom section there, and with respect to the English, it's on page 9 of the English translation, and it is -- if you see where it says "You see the first thing ...", that paragraph, there is a sentence that is underlined. It begins with "There is no way ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask that he put to the witness the entire quotation because they're taking it halfway out of context, which I believe is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, formulate your objection again with greater precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honours. We have this alleged article, for which we don't have the publication date. Essentially, it is a written statement by this -- they've now identified Mr. Matkovic, who is out of court, is not here. They're presenting the document which has not been admitted into evidence up until today's date. They are presenting this to present this as a statement of Milan Lukic as this witness, this Matkovic has said, he said X, Y, and Z. During the Prosecution's case in chief, we presented signed, sworn statements under oath and under penalty of perjury produced by this Office of the Prosecutor, produced by witnesses who were Prosecution witnesses, evidence by Prosecution investigators who were Prosecution witnesses. When we tried to present those documents that were quite explicit in terms of doing the exact same thing Mr. Groome is trying to do with this article, putting it to the witness to challenge their testimony as to Milan Lukic's acts, deeds, and character, we were told by the Trial Chamber we could not. In fact, on the objection of Mr. Groome, we were denied that opportunity. And therefore now we have a certain number of the Prosecution's witnesses on our witness list that we have had to call as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the written statement, just to have them verify the written statement that go against our 45-witness quota. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this in the form of a statement, the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not, but I believe it amounts to the same thing. It's even weaker than a statement. It's not under oath, it's not delineated as to who is saying what, and they're trying to introduce it now without knowing when it was published, without having the author here to say when it was published, how it was undertaken, and they're trying to present it in the same manner that we tried to use sworn statements, and I think if that manner is not good enough for a sworn statement, it definitely ought not to be good enough for this, and I take issue with Mr. Groome testifying as a witness as he is so apt to do in this case about what Duga magazine is. Let's bring someone in, let's find out what the magazine is, what its reputation is, who its publishers are, et cetera, if we really want to go down that road. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the problem here is that we're talking about a very narrow, a very specific exception to hearsay, to the hearsay rule. If this was an unpublished notes or statement or any other document by this journalist, of course I would not be allowed to put it to this witness, but it's not. It's something that is published, and this witness has testified as to Mr. Lukic's good character. I brought with me what's considered a -- I think my American colleagues will recognize it as a very authoritative source on evidence, and it's McCormick's on Evidence. If I might, if the Chamber -- I don't want to insult the Chamber, but if the Chamber would find it helpful, I'd be willing to read the paragraph that deals precisely with this type of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, they don't have a date of publication. They cannot prove it was published. They don't have a certificate of publication. They don't have the author to say it was published. They have a document that they are presenting, a document out of context. They don't have the original newspaper, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's authenticity you are questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Authenticity and relevance and admissibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit with respect to the authenticity argument, the Chamber's able to look at the copy of the document and assess for itself. It has pictures. It has -- with respect to the context, if you'll read the context, it gives some sense of the time period. It's my belief that it was published in November of 1992. Again, it is a matter that I'm still investigating, but I believe there's nothing improper with putting the newspaper article to this witness to test or to challenge his assessment of Mr. Lukic's credibility or character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Just to clarify our objection, we join the objection of the Milan Lukic team regarding authenticity, the relevance, and the admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it you wanted to read from McCormick?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's McCormick on Evidence. Again, Your Honour, I don't mean to insult the Chamber. It's a paragraph, if the Chamber would -- I refreshed my memory about the law in this area before today, so I'm happy to read it if the Chamber finds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is page 348 of McCormick's, it's also section 191 for people with other editions. "Ordinarily if the defendant choses to -- "

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. "Ordinarily, if the defendant chooses to inject his character into the trial in this sense, he does so by producing witnesses to testify to his good character. By relating a personal history supportive of good character, however, the defendant may achieve the same result. Whatever the method, once the defendant gives evidence of pertinent character traits to show that he is not guilty, his claim of possession of these traits and only these traits is open to rebuttal by cross-examination or direct testimony of Prosecution witnesses. "The Prosecution may cross-examine a witness who has testified to the accused's reputation in order to probe the witness's knowledge of the community opinion, not only generally, but specifically as to whether the witness has heard that the defendant has committed particular prior criminal acts that conflict with the reputation vouched for on direct examination. Likewise, if a witness gives his opinion of defendant's character, then the Prosecution can allude to pertinent bad acts by asking whether the witness knew of these matters in forming his opinion." Your Honour, the 65 ter summary of this witness clearly identifies the witness as a character witness. I believe evidence has been led that clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not in issue. I mean, if he puts the character of the accused in issue, then clearly, you can rebut it. That's not the question here. The question is whether this particular piece of evidence that you are seeking to use to rebut it is admissible. Of course you're entitled to rebut it, but the question is whether this particular piece of evidence is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided not to allow the particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to then move on to another area. You have a number of criminal cases before the courts of Serbia. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If we're going to be doing the same thing that Mr. Groome is doing with the witnesses for Mr. Cepic for the defence of Sredoje Lukic, if he has some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you objecting to now? I mean, he's asking him about cases that he has before the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He's asking about a specific type of cases, Your Honour, if he says criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have to wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, do you want me to repeat the question, or did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the question. In the territory of Serbia, among the court cases that I had was the one involving the traffic accident. I was defended by Mr. Cepic, attorney at law. The other two cases are still at the stage of trial or examination, and it doesn't mean that the allegations are proven. Any criminal to meet me in the street, well, I'm retired now. It doesn't mean that these cases have been proven, but at any rate, this is all in Serbia and it's not relevant for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I fully agree with you that until a judgement is entered against you, you are presumed to be innocent. Nevertheless, I do want to ask you some questions. Now, I want to respect your right not to incriminate yourself with respect to any pending case here, so I'm going to ask you a few precisely focussed questions that will not require you to say anything that can be used against you in any of the pending matters, okay? And I'd ask you if I talk about a matter that is still pending, please let me know that it is pending because it is not completely clear to me which cases are closed and which cases are still spending. The first case I want to talk about is an indictment that you have against you that was issued in 20th of March, this year. Do you know the indictment that I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know the indictment that I am speaking about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You have to tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are now embarking on an area of questioning that I must strenuously object to. We've now heard that it's an indictment, that it's not any type of judgement. We've heard that it's for assault. Under the rules of every other legal jurisdiction that I've ever been licensed to practice in front of, the only types of crimes that can be raised or any types of criminal that can be raised against a witness to test their credibility are those going towards crimes of dishonesty. This is not the type of proceeding that can be brought to judge and assess the credibility of a witness, and therefore it is improper. Mr. Groome knows that. He's from the same national jurisdiction I'm from. He knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind the national jurisdiction. Mr. Groome, what are you hoping to achieve by eliciting this kind of evidence if the case has not yet reached the stage of a decision on guilt or innocence? What is it that you are hoping the Trial Chamber will draw from this? What can we properly draw from this kind of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, under 90(H) I'm required to put these allegations or any allegations I want to seek to have the Chamber rely on to the witness. The pending cases, as far as I can tell, are in their last stages of resolution. It is quite possible that before you conclude the evidence in this case that the Prosecution in his rebuttal case will be introducing certificates of conviction. It seems to me that it's -- what I'm -- I should be doing at this stage is simply put the allegation, allow this man to either say, that is me, that is not my case, and then if it comes to pass that before the evidence in this case is concluded that in the rebuttal I'm able to produce a certificate of conviction, then I will have fulfilled my obligation under 90 (H) to actually put it to the man what it is that he had -- the crime. It's not my intention to ask him to make any denial, to make any statement about that but simply confirm the case that is pending against him. And Your Honour, I would also just say, Mr. Markovic has expressed his desire not to do this in public. I have no objection to, at least with respect to the pending cases, handling the matter in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So if I understand you, then, you don't have specific definite information now as to whether these cases have reached a verdict, but you may have that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have information that there is a judgement in one of them, Your Honour. The other two are pending and are in the courts now, and are -- it is quite possible that they could be resolved prior to the conclusion of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have information that there's a judgement in one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you can put that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to put that one as well as the other ones, as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would only add --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one other relevant piece of information I'd like to provide the Chamber, but I think we can do it in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to be brief. I find it wholly inconsistent for Mr. Groome on the one hand to wave McCormick's and then not five minutes later to seek for material to be brought into this case that is explicitly prohibited by McCormick's in the same rules that he has so valiantly tried to push for. Again, I submit that this type of act which is a -- if I read -- reading the indictment, it appears to be a misdemeanor, a misdemeanor that does not relate to any acts of dishonesty, cannot even, if there is a conviction, be used to try to impeach a witness. It goes against the very nature of due process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is not relevant. Here it is a matter of the weight that we attach to it. We are not governed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you cannot consider it, it does matter. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. There is nothing prohibiting us from not considering it. It goes to weight. Stop citing national rules of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologize, Your Honour, but it's been my experience in this very same Tribunal that that type of evidence is not available, but if you rule, you rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In my view, he can put to the witness the case in which there is a conviction and should not put the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say just one other thing in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If that's Your Honour's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for the opportunity. Mr. Groome has proffered this document that is -- it's a two-part document. It's an official not of an interview of the witness conducted by the MUP of Serbia and an interview of another party to those proceedings that are not subject to a conviction. Mr. Groome stated to Your Honours and represented to Your Honours that this was being presented for the purposes of confronting the witness with a contradiction as to his ownership in a cafe. Albeit hastily, I have looked through the transcript and Mr. Groome's cross-examination, and the only reference I see is at page 27, lines 11 through 15, talking about a cafe. That cafe that Mr. Groome asked about is not to be found anywhere in either the B/C/S original nor the English translation of the statement that Mr. Groome is now presenting to be used with this witness for that purpose. I would therefore object because it cannot be used for that way if he hasn't asked him anything about it. Secondly, I have a problem with the translation which Mr. Groome is relying upon. It states it is a draft translation. It won't read who it's done by, but it appears to be done by the Office of the Prosecutor and the problem that I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel kindly slow down, please, for the interpreters and enunciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. The problem that I have with the statement is that on page 1 of the English which appears at, I believe, page 2 of the B/C/S, we have the last full paragraph where it indicates another location, not this cafe that Mr. Groome has asked about, but another location and in parentheses it says Markovic's place in Bulic. The problem I have with this, Your Honour, that phrase, Markovic's place in Bulic, is not to be found anywhere in the B/C/S original. So I submit to you either Mr. Groome is presenting faulty evidence to you or we need to call the Prosecutor as a witness to determine what this information is based upon because again it's not in the B/C/S original at all. So that would be another grounds for objecting to the use and presentation of this statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, since you're appearing before us and will quite frequently be making submissions, please note what the interpreter said. It's on the transcript. Would counsel kindly slow down for the interpreters and enunciate. So it's not just the speed. It's the enunciation of the words. You tend to, I think, bite up your words or to chew them, and they get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I apologize to Your Honours and the translators. I tried very hard during the direct examination to speak slowly and enunciate and it's sometimes easier when I have a game plan as opposed to when I'm speaking off the cuff, as it were, based upon documents I'm just reviewing for the first time in open court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must first say before I deal with the substance that it is very unfortunate that this Court now is being used regularly as a venue on unsubstantiated slander. I've just being accused of falsifying evidence and possibly becoming a witness. I assure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand Mr. Ivetic to be saying that, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you would give me a moment, because I think I've tolerated this about as much as any advocate should have to tolerate it. "So I submit to you that either Mr. Groome is presenting faulty evidence to you or we need to call the Prosecutor as a witness to determine what this information is based upon." That's at 70, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Finish the quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Faulty evidence there I take to mean evidence that is subject to objection. I don't think it means that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, and Your Honours, if you finish the sentence, I'm specifically talking about what's not in the B/C/S original. That's what I'm limiting myself, to and show me where it is in the B/C/S original and I'll withdraw the objection, but it's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed. Since we have it clarified, Mr. Groome, there's no suggestion that you were presenting false evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just for an explanation of -- we still are not in possession of a 65 ter witness list of the Defence. We learned these names last Thursday. We attempted to get information, and we had translators working over the weekend, so if they are not up to the standard that Mr. Ivetic would require, there are two things that can be done. Please give us a list of the witnesses so that we can begin our preparations; and secondly, I am happy any time there's a dispute over translation to sit down with Defence counsel and attempt to resolve it. But I suspect that as long as we're being given such short notice about the schedule for which the witnesses are called, there will be a reoccurring problem of having draft translations that are not as precise and accurate as CLSS translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, your 65 ter list has still not been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We filed our 65 ter list -- what date? -- 19th of November, Your Honour, and Mr. Markovic was tendered as part of the alibi submissions and his ID number was on the original statement presented to the Prosecution, so we would assume they knew exactly who he was. And he's had it since the 7th of July, 2008, regarding this witness, according to the e-mail that we have with the English and B/C/S translations attached in PDF format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you speaking of wider list that was presented by the Defence or another list?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 65 ter list that was submitted, I forget the exact date, was rejected by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it stands with over 90 witnesses, Your Honour. The Chamber -- I was going to raise it with the Chamber tomorrow, but if it's convenient I'll raiser it now, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't want to digress too much from the point, but we come back to that because the Chamber rejected it and ordered you to present a more abbreviated list, and that is what has not been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the thing is, just with this witness, Your Honour, not to be too far afield, we would submit that this witness was notified well in advance of this. Like I said, we believe the statement with the personal ID number was back in July, so the particular allegation with regards to the OTP, I don't think would be relevant to this witness anyway. We are attempting to pare it down, and that's what we've been doing, and Your Honour, that's why we traveled to the region even trying to do that further because we think the original list was submitted for notice purposes as much as anything because we know we have to get everything in at the front side. So we would consider it overinclusive from that standpoint, but you know, we are taking to heart the Court's requirements because we think the case should be pared down as well. We're just doing some of our due diligence as we're moving along, Your Honour. Yeah, and the Thursday deadline, we believe we complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem for the Prosecutor is that over the recess the Prosecution has to prepare for 45 witness that they're not required until the 5th of January to come and tell you that they're not calling. I believe that's prejudicial to the Prosecution. It also is at a tremendous waste of resources. I believe they should be required to prior to the recess to at least let us know who are the 45 witnesses on their witness list so we can begin adequate preparations and not waste --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How does this affect this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have digressed. We'll come back and deal with that matter tomorrow. Now, where are we on this point? Mr. Groome, did you reply to the point made by Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure which point, Your Honour. Perhaps I got lost in the digression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Remember you had wanted to submit a statement and he objected to the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe the Chamber has indicated that it will rule on that. Mr. Ivetic is correct that I used the name of a cafe which may be different from this, so I would seek to -- that's an inadvertent error. Let me put to the gentleman, does he have an ownership in any bar. I put a specific reference to it. If he says he has no ownership interest in any bar, then I believe the statement is very relevant. If he says I do and I have a -- then I believe my introduction of the statement is no longer relevant, and I'll withdraw my attempt to work with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, I just want to say what I intend to do with respect to the marked for identification is simply show that to the witness and ask him, does he recognize that as the indictment that's pending against him. It seems to me without doing that, the whole purpose of having it marked for identification seems to be lost. I'll ask no additional questions other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would remain marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would remain marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you now be shown what's been marked for identification as P 206. I'm not going to ask you any other questions about it other than to ask you, is this the indictment that's pending against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In respect of Mr. Markovic's wishes, I'd ask that we go into private session for this point unless the Chamber feels that it should be done in public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you've mentioned that you were in an accident in 2003. Have you been convicted of a crime arising out of what you call an accident?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, we still object that the type of the crime that is at issue would not be one that would rise to a level of attacking the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, but, it's a matter of weight that we attach to it. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was merely convicted of that crime which was -- which had to do with traffic safety because of the crash in which I was involved in December 2007, and that was brought to completion before the 5th Municipal Court in Belgrade. I have no other convictions as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But sir, the underlying conduct that you were convicted of is that you were driving while drunk and you drove into a fuel tanker. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was very tired that evening, and I fell asleep at the wheel. I had passengers in the car. As far as alcohol is concerned, I had two glasses. I don't know what the percentage was because I was unconscious for several hours in hospital, and I don't recall the crash itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you have now exceeded the time used in examination-in-chief, and you must bring your cross-examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown 06454752, 06454762.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, while that is being brought up so you can take a look at it. You recognize that the judge who heard the case found that your blood alcohol content was three times above the legal limit. You realize that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 0.5 is the legal limit, unless you're a professional driver, in which case there's zero tolerance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've said it's a matter of weight in relation to this kind of evidence. And I particularly, speaking for myself, am not going to attach any great weight to that kind of evidence in terms of the character of the witness. I would advise you to move on to a different area. In any event, you are now about 20 minutes beyond the time used by Mr. Ivetic, and I'll give you another 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd ask, then, that the indictment be -- the judgement be tendered, so I formally tender 06454752 into evidence. I don't have enough time to ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P 208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions. In that case, you testified before the investigating judge and the trial judge that you had one glass of brandy, one drink. You've now said you had two drinks. Was it one drink or two drinks?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, have you not asked him to move on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have. Please move on to another topic, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the final couple of questions I have for you have to do with whether or not you're accurate in your recollection of dates. You seem to be somewhat equivocal on whether Milan Lukic first returned to Visegrad on the 6th of May, and you seem to leave open the possibility that it may have been earlier. But at page 32 of the transcript on line 2, you said: "I don't think that he was" -- meaning he was in Bosnia before -- "because he had just come back from Switzerland." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that he had come from Switzerland and that on the 6th of May we went to Bosnia, that he went to Bosnia with me. Now, I don't know whether he had gone there before. We did not discuss that, so I can't give you any other answer but the one that I gave you, that he went there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did he return from Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in late April, early May. I had seen him a couple of days before the 5th when he told me that his wife [as interpreted] was sick and he had to go down and fetch her. He told me he had returned a couple of days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And your evidence is that when you went to Visegrad, he was forcibly inducted into the police reserves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was going to wait for the answer. There's a transcript issue at line 17. It's not his wife, his mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that is so, then we'll take note of that, and please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I got a little bit confused listening to what the Defence was saying. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's your evidence that when you went to Visegrad with him, he was forced to remain there to serve on the reserve police force or the police force. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you whether he was forced, whether he had to. I will tell you this. Every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Serbia and so on had to comply with the military obligation either in the army or in the police. He was told at the check point to report there and he went to the duty officer. I really don't know what his obligation was, whether this was some kind of compulsory service in the reserves. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you are sure that it was the police and not the army that he was required to serve in?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the war assignment was, as it is called, because in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, the situation is like this. Those who do their military service in the police then go to the reserve force in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I just have time for a couple of specific questions. I really don't have time to ask you about the general state of affairs. I want to ask you to take a look at a document from the Sredoje Lukic -- that was brought to this court by the Sredoje Lukic team, and it is 2D040413, and I'd ask that that document be placed on the screen, and if we could go straight to a page that is Y 0268242 and bears that number on the upper right-hand corner. Sir, while this is being called up, this title of this document is list of military personnel of the 2nd and 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. First of all, this witness has not shown any personal knowledge. There's no foundation for this document being brought up. Thirdly, and I find no other way to bring this up except to just state it. Mr. Groome is showing a lack of understanding of how the system works. Maybe it's because they didn't call an expert as to how the reserve system works over there, but this document is irrelevant as to what this witness testified about in these proceedings in the time period that he specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly that's a matter for redirect and argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that we go to the B/C/S original with Y 0268242 at the top page, the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, please ensure that if a foundation is necessary for the witness's answer that you lay it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not seeking to introduce this. I'm just seeking to test whether his -- to challenge the accuracy of his assertion that Milan Lukic was a member of the police. Is it possible to -- Your Honour, there seems to be some technical difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I could put this to you and when the technical difficulty is resolved. According to this document which, again, it's the Defence of Sredoje Lukic that have brought this to the Court, according to this document, Milan Lukic was a member of this Brigade of the Bosnian Serb Army from the 16th of April, 1992, and until the 1st of July, 1994. So my question to you, sir, if this document is accurate, do you admit, then, that you are wrong when you assert that Milan Lukic was a member of the police force as of the 6th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, how can he speak to its accuracy? You haven't asked him any questions to let us know whether he's able to speak to the accuracy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I know that he's not able to. What I'm putting to him, Your Honour, is that if this document were found to be an accurate document, again, it was brought by the Defence, I don't know much about his providence, I believe it was obtained through an RFA, but I'm asking him whether he's still certain in light of this information whether Milan Lukic was a member of the police force, as he has testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I don't find that approach helpful at all. Please ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown P 150. This is Milan Lukic's statement to the police on the 27th of October, 1992, and I'd ask that we go to the last page of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, being a friend of Milan Lukic, do you recognize his signature there on the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If we can have -- the Prosecution has already raised for purposes of other things in these proceedings the need to have an expert handwriting analysis to testify as to documents. They can't have it both ways, Your Honours. Either one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not with you on that. If he knows his signature, he can say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So then can my witnesses testify about Risto Perisic's signature, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see why not. He can say whether he knows his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, sir, I don't even know how my wife signs her name, let alone Milan Lukic. We never wrote to each other in all these years. I'm really sorry, I don't know his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Mr. Groome, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it really your evidence that you would not be able to recognize your wife's signature?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know she writes in Cyrillic, but I don't really pay attention to it. I don't know how my wife writes or even my children. There are lots of similar handwritings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read you a quote. This document is in evidence. I want to read you a quote of what Milan Lukic said about when he arrived in Visegrad and then ask you whether it changes your view about what you believe to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object as to lack of foundation, and I don't believe Witness 142 testified as to this was what Milan Lukic said. I don't think this was actually anything like that, and in particular, I don't think it was an official statement and it was denied by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is in evidence and it records his statement in the first person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But the fact of the matter is this witness has no ability, and this would again go against the Court's earlier rulings of using one witness's statement against another.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't know how to respond to that, Your Honour. I don't quite understand it. This is a statement of the accused that has now been admitted into evidence. I'm seeking -- it contradicts the evidence of a witness before the Court. I'm simply seeking to put the statement that's in evidence before a witness who's before the Court and to question him about whether that contradiction makes him reconsider his testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it also represents a summary and notes of a 9-hour interview, not an actual statement as we would traditionally understand it. This was the one that went overnight into the wee hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is actually not that statement. This is the one taken by the police. If you recall, that witness took a long interview and we had his notes. What we're talking about here is the police statement taken by the Uzice police at the time of his arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, tell us exactly what is it that you are seeking to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness is mistaken when he gives his account about what happened when he returned with Milan Lukic on the 6th of May. I think he's incorrect about the date. I think he's incorrect about what happened. Here, we have a statement by Mr. Milan Lukic giving another date and giving another organization that he was part of in Visegrad, not the police. I believe it's entirely proper to put it to the witness, either to refresh his recollection that he's made some mistake in his testimony or to put it to him that he is in fact wrong, that he did not appreciate the reality of when Mr. Lukic returned or for whom he worked when he returned. I believe it's an entirely proper line of questioning with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can be heard, this is a very serious matter, then, because what Mr. Groome is now asking to do is precisely what Mr. Groome's office prevented us from doing. Witness VG-64, trans -- page 2902, when we tried to present the sworn statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor of the husband of the protected witness, Ms. Maxine Marcus, and objected precisely to us using it to either refresh the recollection of the witness or to confront them with contradictory testimony. So we were not permitted the opportunity to use that statement. Mr. Groome is now trying to have the backside of it, to enjoy the fruits that he prevented us from having in his case in chief. I believe it's wholly improper and goes against the rule of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fundamental difference, though, and the critical difference is is that the evidence is between the two people that are here. It's not taking one witness and then presenting it to a witness who's not here. Here it is. He's saying that he had a conversation. He had dealings with the man here in court. The man here in court has said on a prior occasion what he was, what he was doing, and it completely contradicts this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you accept that distinction, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have a sworn statement. By the way this is a statement that was taken -- if it's the one I'm thinking about, the witness testified that this statement is illegal in Serbian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The statement here is a statement of the accused, who's a party to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. He is entitled to his right not to testify if he so chooses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That makes a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They can't force him to testify, can they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to force him to testify. It's a prior statement that's in evidence. It's a piece of evidence that's in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's a piece of evidence that's -- the statement that we had from the Office of the Prosecutor was a sworn statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor that directly contradicted the witness at that time about the identity of Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly if I was somehow able to have the uniform that Milan Lukic wore in those days and it was a military uniform, I'd be entitled to put it before Mr. Markovic and say, this isn't a police uniform, is it? That would be entirely proper. And it's analogous to what I'm trying to do here except it's the statement of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's irrelevant because again Mr. Groome is not paying attention to the nuances of reserve service in the former Yugoslavia and how that is accomplished, and I submit if he just had a uniform, he could not do it. But I suppose he could ask the question of the witness without the document, but I really think what we're doing is basically saying that the Prosecution can do it one way and the Defence has to do it another way, and that is -- I'm finding it patently unfair that throughout this case we try to use statements of nonparties including persons -- if you might recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Statements of non-parties. Mr. Lukic is a party to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I don't think that that distinction makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read you what Milan Lukic said about when he returned to Visegrad and what he did, and my question to you is going to be, does this change your testimony about what you have said about this matter. "I have been on the front in Visegrad and its surroundings since the 10th of April, 1992. I am the commander of a group called the Avengers, initially known as the Obrenovac Detachment. The group has between 20 and 50 men and is under the command of the Visegrad Territorial Defence, and I am directly subordinate to Vinko Pandurevic." Sir, now that I have put that to you, does that change your testimony about what occurred on the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It does not. I am absolutely sure I'm telling the real truth. Milan, when he met with me, told me he had arrived a few days ago from Switzerland, but whether he had been in the territory of Bosnia before, whether he had returned there earlier, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let's not repeat anything. If the words of your good friend don't persuade you that you might be mistaken, is there any piece of evidence that you would look at and possibly acknowledge that you night be mistaken about the date the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing that question, Mr. Groome. That's comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, transcript page 1321 records you as telling us that Milan Lukic had a light breakfast on the morning of May 6th, 16th years ago. Do you really recall, as you sit here today, recall what Milan Lukic had for breakfast 16 years ago?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: An omelette, an omelette, a cheese omelette, whereas I had an njegus steak. I offered to treat him to this delicacy which I know he had not had any for a long time, but he was an athlete. He had his own strict diet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that your evidence in this regard and the dates that you've testified to is not only improbable, it's unreliable, that your evidence cannot be relied on with respect to the dates that you have given us, beginning of May and June 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th. Do you understand what I am putting to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're putting to me. I can only repeat that my testimony on these dates is truthful, and that's what I know about Milan Lukic. It's completely truthful. It's another matter that I cannot confirm anything with regard to events that transpired later, but what I said is completely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. No questions from the Defence of Sredoje Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologize, Your Honours. Mr. Markovic, on behalf of the Defence of Milan Lukic and Milan Lukic himself, I thank you for coming today. I have no questions for redirect. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank all counsel and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, when was this indictment laid, the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The indictment that was marked for identification, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. The indictment against Milan, Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I personally am bad with dates. I'd prefer to check, if I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I wanted to ask you, when did you first learn of these charges against your friend Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When an international all-points alert was issued and the indictment was raised by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So when was that? How long ago?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: A couple of years ago. I don't know. I know that there was an indictment not only against him but against several people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I wanted to find out, if you had all this information that would be beneficial to your friend, why did you keep it to yourself? Did you go to the authorities to provide them with this information which could exculpate Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, from 1997 I had no further contact with Milan Lukic, especially when he was no longer in Visegrad, and at the time when this international indictment was brought against him, I had nothing -- no useful information on him to help the authorities with. I knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you knew about the charges against him. Were you not aware of the charges that had been laid against him in the indictment, the allegations that he was at a particular place on a particular date doing these very bad things that were alleged, and you would have had information that he was somewhere else, and so I'm asking, why didn't you go to the authorities with that information?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The authorities knew everything about the international search for him. At that time, I wasn't working. In 2003, I was on a prolonged sick leave in various spas and sanitoria, hospitals. I spent a long time in hospital. At any rate, I had no information to give. If as a police officer I had such information, I would have helped the authorities and I would have even arrested him as a police officer. I would have done whatever my duty was to do. I had the occasion in my life to arrest a person with whom I was on very good terms with. I took that former minister, actually, in a former government to the police station to give a statement. So whoever it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's not digress. The first time that you spoke about Milan being with you at another place in relation to these charges, is that when you would have been approached by the lawyers for Milan?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. What I'm trying to find out is, when was the first time that you made any statement to anybody concerning Milan being with you at certain places?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke for the first time about it to Lawyer Lakcevic from his Defence team, and I told him only the things I know. I knew nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that information you'd have had all along from 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Milan was in Visegrad from 1992 after the war. He lived in Visegrad. Nothing was being concealed there. There were S4 units there at the time. If there had been something, I suppose they would have arrested him. What information did I have? I had no information about him after my last contact with him. At the time when this international search started, I had nothing on him. I couldn't even call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell what you're trying to get at, and what concerns me is is that what had not been established either on direct, cross, or I even think with your query is that this witness had actually read the indictment. It's one thing to get news reports that there is an indictment and even some general allegations as to what those indictment might have consisted about, but actually have read the indictment and see the relevant dates and periods, I think you're asking is why didn't he come forward with exculpatory, and he keeps responding as if it should have been information to arrest him. And I think that from the time period involved, that's what he keeps responding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, he keeps using the word "potjernica," which is the arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, that concludes your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it and you may now leave. In any event, we are going to adjourn for the day, so you will leave with us. ---Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m., To be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of December, 2008, at 8.50 a.m.
